clue.text: Inspector again involved in painful affair of the heart

indicators.note: things that are involved are tangled together, so the letters get mixed up

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter as the fodder

explanation.surface: A police inspector caught up once more in a painful romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affair of the heart' suggests romance; here it is literal, a medical condition of the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Angina pectoris is chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the cardiac muscle, a literally painful heart complaint.

clue.text: New warden with proposal for 10

indicators.note: making something new means remaking it, so the following word is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a motion is a proposal put to a meeting

explanation.surface: A newly appointed warden puts forward a proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 down is POET LAUREATE; Andrew Motion held that post from 1999 to 2009.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Motion was the British Poet Laureate for a decade, the holder of the cross-referenced post.

clue.text: Snap of teeth with sound of bow on string

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the grinding or snapping together of teeth
second meaning: a fanciful description of the harsh grating noise of a badly drawn violin bow

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is loose: a scraping bow on a fiddle string makes a grating, teeth-on-edge noise.
explanation.definitionFit: To grind or clash the jaws together angrily is the core sense, extended to any harsh grating noise.

clue.text: Fruit of blunder in battle

indicators.note: one item placed in another sits inside it, so the first piece goes within the second

parts.note: Naseby, the 1645 battle of the English Civil War
to err is to blunder

explanation.surface: The result of a mistake made during a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Naseby is a village in Northamptonshire, site of the decisive Civil War battle; ERR goes between NASE and BY. 'Fruit of' looks like 'consequence of'.
explanation.definitionFit: The naseberry is the sapodilla, a sweet brown tropical fruit grown in the Caribbean.

clue.text: No tea served up on local transport

parts.note: a local is a pub, abbreviated PH for public house

indicators.note: in a down entry, served up means sent upwards, so the words are read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that the local bus has no tea on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is British slang for one's nearby pub, abbreviated PH on maps.
explanation.definitionFit: A phaeton is a light open horse-drawn carriage, a means of transport in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Many bankrupt after company fire

indicators.note: after places the preceding word's piece behind the one that follows it in the clue

parts.note: standard abbreviation for company
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a large number
to go bust is to go bankrupt

explanation.surface: Plenty of firms go bust after a fire destroys a business.
explanation.walkthrough: M as the Roman thousand stands in for 'many'; 'fire' is a verb here, not the blaze in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To combust is to burn or catch fire, so it fits fire used as a verb.

clue.text: Before getting this, bearings start to be heated

definitions.text: Before getting this, bearings start to be heated

parts.words: Before getting this, bearings start to be heated
parts.note: surface reading: machine bearings running dry begin to overheat until lubricated
setter's reading: a drinker becomes warm and flushed before getting drunk

explanation.surface: A mechanic notes that dry bearings run hot until they are lubricated.
explanation.walkthrough: The word works both for lubricated machinery and, in slang, for someone who is drunk; heated hints at the flushed drinker too.
explanation.definitionFit: Bearings get lubricated to stop them overheating, and in slang a tipsy person is also described this way.

clue.text: Ecumenical feature of the cross?

definitions.note: an adjective cluing a verb, read jokily as inter-sect, between sects
definitions.meaning: first meaning, punning: split into Latin 'between' plus a religious group, so shared between denominations

definitions.note: a noun phrase for what the two bars of a cross do
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the two bars of a cross meet and pass through each other

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a pun: ecumenical means bringing churches together, and the answer split in two reads 'between sects'. The question mark flags the liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: Two lines that cross each other meet at a point, which is exactly what the bars of a cross do.

clue.text: A script given by physician for nightcaps?

parts.note: standard abbreviation for doctor
taken as written
MS is short for manuscript, a handwritten script

explanation.surface: A doctor writes out a prescription for something to help sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Script' suggests a prescription, fitting the doctor; here it is a manuscript. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightcap is an alcoholic drink before bed, and small measures of whisky are often taken this way.

clue.text: Weapon with a jolly, blazing sound

parts.note: taken as written
a Jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM

indicators.note: the sound of a word is what is heard, so the spelling may change as long as the pronunciation is kept

parts.note: blazing means on fire, alight; written in the brand-name spelling

explanation.surface: A gun that goes off with a cheerful, fiery bang.
explanation.walkthrough: Jolly as a noun is old naval slang for a Royal Marine. The Armalite is a make of rifle, its name spelt in trademark style.
explanation.definitionFit: The Armalite is a lightweight American assault rifle, a firearm and therefore a weapon.

clue.text: A true tale adapted by US writer, or 1 down

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American writer

indicators.note: a story adapted for another medium is reworked, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the three words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A real-life story reworked by an American author.
explanation.walkthrough: POE comes first and the rearranged letters follow. 1 down is ANDREW MOTION, who held the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Motion was appointed the official national poet of the United Kingdom, the honorary post named here.

clue.text: Show, a one-time hit, put over in the same location

parts.note: an ex is a former partner, so ex means one-time

indicators.note: something put over another covers it on both sides, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: taken as written
IB is short for ibidem, Latin for in the same place

explanation.surface: A revival of a former hit show, staged in the same venue.
explanation.walkthrough: IB (ibid.) is the scholarly abbreviation used in footnotes for 'in the same place'; HIT wraps around it.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhibit something is to put it on display, which is what showing it means.

clue.text: Suffer from insufficient energy

parts.note: under as a prefix means not enough, as in underfed
go means energy or vigour, as in full of go

explanation.surface: Someone is unwell because of a lack of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suffer from' reads as a single phrase, but 'from' is only the link.
explanation.definitionFit: To undergo an ordeal is to experience or endure it, close to suffering it.

clue.text: Stingy character of motorway service having lost its grip

indicators.note: having lost something means it has been taken away, so letters are removed

parts.note: M as in the M1, the British motorway prefix
taken as written
a vice is a tool that grips a workpiece

explanation.surface: A mean-spirited figure running a motorway service area that has gone downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing VICE from SERVICE leaves SER. British motorways are numbered with M, like the M25.
explanation.definitionFit: A miser hoards money and refuses to spend it, the very type of a stingy person.

clue.text: What one might do at a brasserie or brassiere

definitions.text: What one might do at a brasserie
definitions.note: split as SUP PORTER, a verb phrase
definitions.meaning: first meaning: drink a dark beer at a bar-restaurant, split into two words
second meaning: an undergarment that holds up the bust

explanation.walkthrough: Brasserie and brassiere differ by two swapped letters; split one way the answer is drinking a beer, read whole it is a bra.
explanation.definitionFit: To sup porter is to drink a dark beer; a bra is a garment that holds up and props the bust.

clue.text: Grub — could it turn men crazy?

indicators.note: a crazy arrangement is a disordered one, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: three words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: Wondering whether some food might drive men mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' looks like an anagram signal, but it is fodder; the signal is 'crazy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Grub is informal for food, and nutriment means nourishing food that sustains life.

clue.text: Rise in building material around last Easter

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: cement is a building material

indicators.note: last asks for only the final letter of the next word

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Building costs went up around the end of Easter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise in' reads like a single phrase, but 'in' contributes its own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An increment is an increase or added amount, such as a step up in salary.

clue.text: Baker's selection of tacky pies?

indicators.note: a selection is a mixed assortment, so the letters are taken in a new order

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A baker's assortment of rather tasteless pastries.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue serves as both definition and wordplay: the baker's choice is a dessert rearranged from tacky pies, and its sticky, boozy sponge is literally tacky.
explanation.definitionFit: Tipsy cake is a dessert of sponge soaked in wine or sherry, something a confectioner might offer.

clue.text: Possibly ban Asti — and other drinks!

definitions.text: Possibly ban Asti — and other drinks!

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters may be reordered

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A teetotal call to prohibit Italian sparkling wine and all other alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: Asti is a sparkling Italian wine; the whole clue describes what a teetotaller does as well as giving the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to refrain from alcohol altogether, effectively banning every drink for oneself.

clue.text: Interpreter, for example, in late summer abroad

parts.note: late in the sense of former, which is ex
standard abbreviation for for example
été is French for summer

explanation.surface: A translator working overseas at the end of summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late summer' reads as a season, but 'late' and 'summer' give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An exegete explains and expounds texts, especially scripture, so is an interpreter of meaning.

clue.text: Priestly wear for short medieval peasant

indicators.note: something short is missing its end, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: a cottar was a peasant holding a cottage in return for labour

explanation.surface: Clerical robes provided for a lowly peasant of the Middle Ages.
explanation.walkthrough: COTTAR, also spelt cotter, loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cotta is a short surplice worn by clergy and choristers, a liturgical garment.

clue.text: Comparisons concerning the nose

definitions.note: a noun cluing an adjective, by allusion to Dogberry's line 'comparisons are odorous'
definitions.meaning: first meaning: Dogberry's malapropism in Much Ado About Nothing
second meaning: to do with smell

explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's constable Dogberry mangles 'comparisons are odious', so the answer is what comparisons are in his line.
explanation.definitionFit: Odorous means having a smell, so it relates to what the nose detects; Dogberry applies it to comparisons.

clue.text: Prognostications provided by women's magazine

indicators.note: the letters are supplied by the following word itself, sitting inside it

parts.note: the word minus its first letter
surface padding, completing the picture of a horoscope page

explanation.surface: Horoscope predictions printed in a women's magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Magazine' completes the picture of horoscope pages but plays no part.
explanation.definitionFit: Omens are signs taken to foretell the future, which is what prognostications are.

clue.text: English reader of old High German

parts.note: standard abbreviation for English
a lector is a reader, especially of lessons in church

explanation.surface: An English lecturer in the historic High German language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old High German' looks like the language; here it is a high-ranking German of old, one of the princes who chose the Holy Roman Emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Electors were German princes entitled to choose the Holy Roman Emperor, so great historic German nobles.

clue.text: Giant free from taint

indicators.note: letters set free are loosed from their order and can fall into a new one

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A colossus who is free of any corruption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free from taint' reads as 'unblemished', but 'free' is the signal and 'from' the link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were the gigantic gods of Greek myth, so a titan is any huge or mighty being.

clue.text: Cheap fare always available in a coach

indicators.note: one item placed in another is enclosed by it, so the first goes inside the second

parts.note: a stage is a stagecoach
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: Budget tickets are always on offer for a coach journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' suggests a ticket price; here it is a class of passenger travel on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Steerage was the cheapest passenger accommodation on a ship, the lowest-priced way to travel.

clue.text: More to be included in the next race at Doncaster

indicators.note: the letters are included within the following words, spanning their boundary

parts.note: spanning the two words, inside them
surface padding naming the racecourse

explanation.surface: An additional runner will be added to the following race at Doncaster.
explanation.walkthrough: Doncaster is a racecourse in Yorkshire; 'at Doncaster' only dresses the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means additional, beyond the usual amount, which is the sense of more.

clue.text: False pretences no sin — but they get the bird

indicators.note: false things are not what they appear, so these letters hide a different arrangement

parts.note: three words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: Fraud is no sin, yet the fraudsters still get booed off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting the bird' sounds like being jeered; here bird is rhyming slang (birdlime, time) for a stretch in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Bird is British slang for prison time, so those who get bird are given custodial terms.
